II 'The phonological system' pp. 12-41: 2.3 Syllable (pp. 36-40: all syllables open, V/CV/CVV, mono- to tetrasyllabic words), 2.4 Tone (pp. 40-41: 'As Poumai is one of the Tibeto-Burman language, it is a tonal language. There are four tones in Poumai': High, Low, Mid (unmarked), High-Low; contour type). No token of 'stress'/'accent'. Variety: Purul village.

sources.note: Nothing. Ch. II Phonology pp. 13-39: 2.3 Syllable (pp. 32-37: open syllables only, CV/CCV/CVV; mono-, di-, polysyllabic words, 'polysyllabic words are very rare'), 2.4 Tone (pp. 37-39: four tones Low, Mid-Falling, Mid-Rising-and-Falling, High-Falling; 'In Poula almost all the words have atleast two tone'). The only token of 'stress' is 'common among linguists to stress lexical relevance' (p. 37). Variety: Saranamai village, Paomata block.

sources.citation: Veikho, Sahiinii Lemaina & Barika Khyriem. 2015. Poula phonetics and phonology: An initial overview. In L. Konnerth, S. Morey, P. Sarmah & A. Teo (eds), North East Indian Linguistics 7, 47-62. Canberra: Asia-Pacific Linguistics (open access, CC-BY). hdl 1885/95392.
sources.note: Nothing. Describes syllable structure (C)V1(V2)T with obligatory tone, no codas, light vs heavy syllables, 25 consonants, 6 monophthongs + 4 diphthongs, and four lexical tones Low 11, Mid-Falling 21, Mid-Rising-and-Falling 231, High-Falling 51 (pp. 49, 59-60). No token of 'stress', 'accent' or 'prominence' anywhere in the chapter; tone study limited to monosyllables. Variety: Naamai (Koide) village, Lepaona block.
